one_liner: Archived C HTTP/1.1 server library on libevent; about 1.15x Boost.Beast's async example on one plaintext wrk test.
what_it_does: libevhtp is an embeddable HTTP/1.0/1.1 server (plus a basic client) in C on libevent 2: you create an evhtp_t on an event_base and register C callbacks by exact path, glob or regex (evhtp_set_cb, evhtp_set_glob_cb, evhtp_set_regex_cb). Handlers write into req->buffer_out and call evhtp_send_reply; chunked replies, per-request pause/resume, vhosts and OpenSSL TLS are built in. It is not a drop-in for Beast: it is a callback framework that owns the accept loop, not a header-only message and stream toolkit on Asio.
how_it_is_fast: evhtp_use_threads_wexit() starts evthr workers, each running its own libevent event_base; the listener thread passes each accepted connection over an AF_UNIX socketpair to the worker with the smallest FIONREAD backlog, so a connection stays on one thread and takes no locks. Requests go through htparse, a byte-at-a-time state machine that checks URI characters against a 256-bit bitmap (usual[]) and acts on Connection, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding while it parses the headers. Replies build the status line and headers with scatter-gather evbuffer iovecs and custom integer-to-ASCII code instead of printf formatting (tagged [PERF] in the ChangeLog). The benchmark server also set EVHTP_FLAG_ENABLE_ALL, which turns on SO_REUSEPORT, TCP_NODELAY and TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT.
when_to_use: A C program already built around a libevent event_base needs an embedded HTTP/1.1 endpoint, such as an admin, metrics or small REST API.
Many keep-alive connections get small fixed responses on a few cores: the benchmark measured 254k req/s on 4 cores against 220k for the Beast async example.
Handlers can keep all per-connection work on the worker thread that owns the connection, like examples/thread_design.c does with async Redis on each worker's event_base.
You are willing to vendor and patch a frozen, BSD-3-Clause codebase of about 8.3k lines (evhtp.c, parser.c, thread.c). On Ubuntu 24.04, libevhtp-dev 1.2.18 also installs from apt.
when_not_to_use: You need HTTP/2, WebSocket or server-sent events: evhtp_proto has only HTTP/1.0 and 1.1, WebSocket support was never merged (#116), and the SSE question (#166) has no answer.

The server faces the internet without a hardened proxy in front. The repo is archived, so no security fixes will come. Parser issues are still open: #131, a URI split across two reads gains a stray character; #161, an invalid Content-Length gets an empty reply.
You serve HTTPS with real response bodies: #160 (open) reports 42,484 req/s falling to 1,012 req/s after adding an 11-byte body over TLS, and a fragmented output buffer is the suspected cause.
You want the highest throughput: in the same table nginx (336k), actix (334k), Drogon (320k) and gofiber with GOMAXPROCS=4 (272k) beat libevhtp, and bun ties it at 254k.
You want idiomatic, header-only C++ with Asio integration, or you target Windows: MinGW build steps are in the README, but Windows build issues #103, #141 and #142 are still open.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake add_library; distro packages ship a shared lib)
integration.dependencies: libevent 2.x (required). Optional: OpenSSL (TLS), pthreads (evthr thread pool), Oniguruma with its POSIX API (regex routes), jemalloc or tcmalloc (EVHTP_ALLOCATOR).
integration.min_toolchain: C99 gcc or clang, CMake 3.1+. The 1.2.18 CMakeLists calls find_package(LibEvent), which misses the CMake config of a self-built libevent 2.1.8 (#135).
integration.platforms: Linux and other POSIX systems (pthreads, AF_UNIX socketpairs, ioctl FIONREAD). No SIMD or architecture-specific code. Windows only via MinGW, with open build issues.
integration.thread_safety: Each connection is pinned to one evthr worker and its event_base, so reply from that thread. Replying from another thread aborts under load (#139). evhtp_use_callback_locks() adds a mutex for changing callbacks and hooks at runtime.

gotchas: Tag 1.2.18 (2019-02-06) is the version Ubuntu ships and the one benchmarked. It predates the develop-branch fixes for bytes skipped in long URIs (#128), and #131 reports that the develop fix adds a stray character instead. Pin a version and test long, fragmented request lines.
By default there are no read/write timeouts and no body-size cap (max_body_size 0 means unlimited). Set evhtp_set_timeouts and evhtp_set_max_body_size, or slow or huge requests hold connections.
EVHTP_FLAG_DEFAULTS turns on only 100-continue. SO_REUSEPORT, TCP_NODELAY and TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT stay off unless you enable them, and the benchmark enabled all of them.

Regex routes need Oniguruma built with --enable-posix-api=yes for onig 6.9.5_rev1 and later (#162). Otherwise CMake prints 'ONIGURUMA NOT FOUND, DISABLING REGEX SUPPORT' and builds without regex routes. evhtp_use_threads() is marked DEPRECATED in favor of evhtp_use_threads_wexit().
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Drogon is faster in the same gonwan table (320k vs 254k req/s) and gives a full C++ framework, so choose libevhtp over Drogon only when you need a plain C API that plugs into an existing libevent event_base. For a new C server, the H2O and Lwan entries have stronger published benchmarks and do not depend on an archived library.
verified_claims_summary: One homemade wrk run (-c1000 -t10 -d30s, keep-alive, GET /text returning 'Hello, World!') against 4-CPU-limited Docker containers on an AMD 7840HS host measured the Ubuntu-packaged libevhtp 1.2.18 on libevent 2.1.12 (4 workers plus a listener) at 254k req/s. On the same setup the Boost 1.83 Beast http_server_async example measured 220k req/s. Both test servers were built with gcc/g++ -O2 from ubuntu:24.04 build-essential. The Beast example runs 4 threads on one shared io_context with per-connection strands, so part of the 1.15x gap may come from how that example is set up.
status_note: The repo is archived and read-only: last commit 2019-08-02, last tag 1.2.18. The original author's fork (ellzey/libevhtp) only merged upstream in 2025 and added no fixes. The BSD-3-Clause license and small C codebase make it practical to vendor and patch, but you would own every security fix.
